newsitem.title: FRANCE: Economists split on BoF rate cut prospects Thurs.
newsitem.headline: Economists split on BoF rate cut prospects Thurs.

text.p: Economists were split on whether the Bank of France would cut rates on Thursday as a show of support to the French government, which presented its 1997 budget on Wednesday.

Those who thought a cut was likely said the Bank had room to bring its floor intervention rate closer to the German repo rate, adding that the Bank would want to show financial markets it believed the government's budget was credible.
The intervention rate is 3.35 percent and the German repo rate is 3.0 percent. The Bank's ceiling five-to-10 day emergency lending rate is 4.75 percent.
"They will deliver a 15 basis-point stamp of approval to yesterday's budget," said Credit Lyonnais economist Iain Lindsay.
"For them not to move at all would be a spit in the face," added Sean Shepley, international economist at CS First Boston.
The Bank of France's monetary policy council will hold a regular meeting on Thursday morning.
Other analysts argued a weaker French franc, which fell nearly a centime against the mark on Wednesday, would make it difficult for the Bank to act so soon after the budget.
They also saw the Bank's failure to lower call money on Thursday morning as a sign the Bank would wait until markets stabilized before making its next move.
Call money, which the Bank uses as a third unofficial rate, has not moved since it was lowered by 1/16 percentage point to 3-7/16-9/16 percent on August 23.
Another factor seen tying the Bank's hands was strong growth in August German M3 money supply released on Thursday morning.

"Since the markets have no real reason to be enthusiastic about the budget and the franc has weakened some, it might push back any rate cuts," said Francois-Xavier Chauchat, market economist at Banque Nationale de Paris.
"They would like to give approval to the budget, but they are limited by the franc's weakness," he added.

"There has been some moderate scepticism about the French budget compared to German austerity measures, and it might be wise to leave it all alone until the dust settles," said Stephen Hannah, economist at IBJ International.
Virtually all the economists asked by Reuters said French rates had room to fall in the months ahead whatever the Bank of France decided to do on Thursday.
Most economists, questioned before the release of the budget, had said the Bank of France would lower rates if the budget were well-received by the market.
